items.question: Under most current copyright frameworks, what is the status of text generated entirely by an AI model with no human creative contribution?

options.A: Copyright vests in the AI model's developer because the developer created the technology that produced the text.
options.B: The text is unlikely to qualify for copyright protection because most frameworks require a human author as a condition of copyright subsisting.
options.C: Copyright vests in the user who composed the prompt, because a prompt is a creative directive that establishes authorship.
options.D: The text is automatically covered by a compulsory licence permitting anyone to use it for non-commercial purposes.

items.question: Which TWO actions should be taken immediately when an AI workflow may have exposed personal data to unauthorised recipients? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Stop the workflow and revoke access to the affected output to prevent further exposure.
options.B: Destroy all records of the incident to minimise regulatory scrutiny.
options.C: Replace the AI model with a lower-tier model while the investigation proceeds.
options.D: Preserve evidence of what was generated, who received it, and what personal data was involved.
options.E: Request an emergency model retrain from the AI vendor within 48 hours.

items.question: Which TWO IP or licensing risks are specific to using AI-generated outputs in a commercial product? (Choose TWO)

options.A: The output may contain more words than the prompt, creating a derivative work obligation.
options.B: The output may reproduce copyrighted expression from training data, exposing the user to infringement claims.
options.C: The output may lack copyright protection because it was generated without human authorship, weakening the product's IP position.
options.D: The model developer automatically holds first-right-of-refusal to acquire any commercial product built using their model's outputs.
options.E: Outputs generated through the API are subject to a different tax treatment than outputs generated through the web interface.

items.question: What does applying least privilege mean in the context of a shared AI Project?

options.A: Each user in the Project should be limited to submitting prompts of no more than a defined word count.
options.B: Each user should be granted access only to the Project contents and capabilities required for their specific role.
options.C: The organisation should use the lowest-tier model available for Project work to control operational cost.
options.D: Project knowledge documents should be limited to a minimum number of pages to reduce information exposure.

items.question: What is the primary goal of employee governance training on AI tools?

options.A: To certify employees as proficient prompt engineers approved to use AI tools without supervision.
options.B: To introduce employees to the features and interface of the organisation's approved AI tools.
options.C: To evaluate whether individual employees are suitable candidates for AI-focused roles.
options.D: To ensure employees understand what data may be submitted, which tools are approved, and what review steps are required before acting on outputs.

items.question: What fairness obligation arises when AI assists in decisions affecting members of a legally protected group?

options.A: The organisation must ensure the AI-assisted process does not produce discriminatory outcomes for protected groups, regardless of whether the bias was intentional.
options.B: The AI tool must be certified as bias-free by a recognised third party before being used in decisions affecting protected groups.
options.C: All AI-assisted decisions affecting protected groups require approval from an independent ethics panel before they are communicated.
options.D: The organisation is exempt from fairness obligations if the AI vendor's terms of service include a standard bias disclaimer.

items.question: Why does data minimisation matter specifically in AI-assisted high-stakes decisions, beyond its general privacy benefit?

options.A: Minimising data reduces model processing time, making high-stakes decisions faster.
options.B: High-stakes decisions always involve regulated data categories that cannot be processed by AI at all.
options.C: Limiting input data to what is necessary reduces the risk that irrelevant or protected attributes inappropriately influence the AI's contribution to the decision.
options.D: Data minimisation is only required when a decision affects more than a defined number of individuals simultaneously.

items.question: How does an audit trail support accountability in an AI-assisted decision that affects an individual?

options.A: It verifies that the AI model's confidence score exceeded a required threshold before the decision was finalised.
options.B: It provides an evidence base showing which human reviewed the AI output, at what time, and what decision was made, enabling the responsible party to be identified and the decision to be explained.
options.C: It automatically notifies the affected individual of the AI's contribution to the decision as soon as the entry is logged.
options.D: It restricts subsequent access to the decision record, preventing post-hoc alteration.

items.question: What compound compliance failure does shadow AI create when an employee uses an unapproved tool to process personal data?

options.A: The personal data may be processed more slowly, leading to quality degradation in outputs.
options.B: The IT department may reject the output on technical grounds because it was not generated by an approved system.
options.C: The personal data becomes subject to the tool's jurisdictional requirements, which the organisation cannot verify without an approved review process.
options.D: The organisation simultaneously violates its data-processing obligations (no DPA with the vendor) and its governance obligations (no approved-tool register entry), creating a layered compliance failure.

items.question: When must an organisation rely on consent as the legal basis for using AI to process personal data in a decision affecting an individual?

options.A: Always — consent is the only lawful basis for any AI involvement in a decision affecting an individual.
options.B: Only when the decision is made by a senior executive rather than an automated system.
options.C: When consent is the only available lawful basis for the processing, or when the applicable framework specifically requires consent for the type of automated processing involved.
options.D: Only when the individual's personal data includes special-category information such as health data.

items.question: When a data breach occurs at an AI vendor that is processing an organisation's personal data, who bears primary accountability to affected individuals?

options.A: The AI vendor, because the breach occurred within the vendor's infrastructure.
options.B: The affected individuals themselves, because they consented to data processing.
options.C: The organisation, as the data controller that chose the vendor and must ensure adequate protections were in place.
options.D: The data protection regulator, which assumes accountability when a breach affects multiple individuals.

items.question: Which TWO governance controls serve BOTH data-handling obligations and high-stakes decision oversight simultaneously? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Increasing the AI model's context window to process more data per decision
options.B: Maintaining an audit trail that records what data was submitted, what the AI produced, and who made the final decision
options.C: Configuring the AI tool to reject prompts containing more than a defined word count
options.D: Ensuring that data submitted to the AI in a decision workflow is limited to what is strictly necessary for the specific determination
options.E: Using a dedicated server for high-stakes workloads to reduce output latency

items.question: What is the correct distinction between disclosure, transparency, and explainability in AI governance?

options.A: Disclosure informs individuals of AI involvement in a specific decision; transparency is the organisation's broader openness about how it uses AI; explainability is the ability to give a meaningful account of why a specific decision was reached.
options.B: Disclosure and transparency are synonymous; explainability is the ability to predict what the AI will decide next.
options.C: Transparency applies only to external communications; disclosure applies only to internal stakeholders; explainability is a model property measured exclusively by the vendor.
options.D: Explainability is the overarching standard that subsumes both disclosure and transparency as narrower obligations within it.

items.question: What is the distinction between a data retention obligation and a data deletion obligation in AI governance?

options.A: Retention and deletion obligations are mutually exclusive — an organisation can comply with only one at a time.
options.B: Retention obligations apply to personal data; deletion obligations apply to commercially confidential data.
options.C: A deletion obligation requires data to be destroyed immediately upon collection; a retention obligation requires it to be kept indefinitely.
options.D: A retention obligation requires keeping data for a minimum specified period for a defined purpose; a deletion obligation requires destroying or anonymising it after a maximum permitted period.

items.question: What is the key difference between an AI acceptable-use policy and an AI ethics framework?

options.A: An acceptable-use policy defines operational rules for employee conduct with specific AI tools; an ethics framework articulates principles and values that guide the organisation's overall approach to AI.
options.B: An ethics framework is a legally binding document; an acceptable-use policy is a voluntary commitment with no enforcement mechanism.
options.C: An acceptable-use policy covers only consumer AI tools; an ethics framework applies to custom-built AI systems.
options.D: The two documents are functionally identical — any organisation that produces one implicitly has the other.

items.question: What governance value does a model card provide during AI tool procurement?

options.A: It specifies the vendor's enterprise pricing tiers and usage limits available to the purchasing organisation.
options.B: It documents the model's intended use cases, known limitations, bias evaluations, and training data characteristics, enabling an informed risk assessment.
options.C: It certifies that the model has passed government security clearance for deployment in regulated public-sector environments.
options.D: It assigns the model a numeric risk rating that automatically determines the required human oversight level.

items.question: How does data minimisation interact with cross-border data transfer governance in AI workflows?

options.A: Minimising data before transfer reduces both the volume of personal data exposed to a different legal jurisdiction and the potential harm if that jurisdiction's protections prove inadequate.
options.B: Data minimisation exempts an organisation from cross-border transfer requirements because minimised data is no longer considered personal data.
options.C: Cross-border transfer requirements apply only to full unedited datasets; minimised datasets are outside the scope of transfer governance.
options.D: Minimising data before transfer is prohibited in some jurisdictions because it may alter the data's evidentiary integrity.

items.question: Which TWO controls simultaneously address sensitive data handling risks AND organisational governance gaps? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Using a higher-tier model to process sensitive data more accurately
options.B: Training employees only in prompt engineering techniques for sensitive topics
options.C: Requiring all AI tool submissions containing personal data to be logged in an access-controlled audit system
options.D: Publishing AI-generated content on an internal intranet rather than externally
options.E: Maintaining a register of approved AI tools specifying which data categories each tool is permitted to process

items.question: What is the key difference between relying on consent and relying on legitimate interest as the legal basis for AI processing of personal data?

options.A: Legitimate interest is a stronger basis than consent and should always be preferred for AI workflows to avoid consent-withdrawal risk.
options.B: Consent requires an affirmative act from the individual and can be withdrawn; legitimate interest is assessed by balancing organisational need against individual rights and does not require individual agreement.
options.C: Consent is available only to public authorities; legitimate interest is the standard basis for private-sector organisations.
options.D: The two bases are interchangeable — an organisation may switch between them after processing has begun without any reassessment.

items.question: When a policy exception permits a team to use an AI tool for high-stakes decisions, what additional governance requirement must accompany the exception?

options.A: The team must reduce its AI submission volume to prevent the tool from being overloaded.
options.B: The AI vendor must be informed that the tool will be used for high-stakes decisions and provide written acknowledgement.
options.C: Every team member must complete a formal AI certification before any high-stakes use under the exception begins.
options.D: The exception must define who reviews AI outputs, what authority they have over the final decision, and what escalation path exists if the AI output is unreliable.

items.question: What is the distinction between accountability and auditability in an AI-assisted decision workflow?

options.A: Accountability is a technical property of the AI model; auditability is a property of the organisation's processes.
options.B: Auditability means the decision can be appealed; accountability means the decision is legally binding.
options.C: Accountability is the obligation of a named party to own and explain the decision outcome; auditability is the property of a workflow that makes it possible to reconstruct and verify what happened.
options.D: The two concepts are equivalent — an auditable system is automatically accountable, and vice versa.

items.question: Which TWO topics must effective employee governance training on AI tools cover to address BOTH data-handling and responsible-use obligations? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Advanced prompt engineering techniques for improving output quality across domains
options.B: Which data categories may and may not be submitted to each approved AI tool
options.C: How to configure AI model parameters such as temperature and top-p sampling
options.D: What review and oversight steps are required before acting on AI outputs in high-stakes contexts
options.E: How to write system prompts that maximise the AI model's compliance with complex instructions

items.question: Which TWO governance principles TOGETHER most directly prevent AI from contributing to an unfair, unexplainable, or data-driven wrong in a consequential decision? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Data minimisation — limiting submitted data to what is necessary so irrelevant or proxy attributes cannot influence the AI's output
options.B: Data residency — ensuring personal data is stored only in approved jurisdictions
options.C: Human oversight — requiring a named human to review the AI's contribution and take accountability for the final determination
options.D: Acceptable-use policy — defining the tools employees are permitted to use
options.E: Storage limitation — deleting personal data after the purpose for which it was collected is served

items.question: What specific risk arises when a model produces a multi-step reasoning chain where each step builds on the prior step's conclusions?

options.A: An error in an early step can propagate through subsequent steps, compounding the total error in the final output
options.B: Multi-step reasoning forces the model to rely on parametric memory for every step except the first
options.C: The model hedges more in multi-step reasoning, making errors more visible and easier to detect
options.D: Each step independently re-verifies the previous one, reducing the cumulative error rate relative to a single step

items.question: What is 'verification theater' in the context of model output quality control?

options.A: Asking the model itself to verify its own output, creating a superficially independent-looking review
options.B: Performing review steps that create the appearance of quality assurance without covering actual risks — such as checking format and grammar while leaving specific factual claims unverified
options.C: Presenting verification results to stakeholders that were generated by automation rather than a human reviewer
options.D: Running multiple model generations and selecting the best-looking output without verifying any of them

items.question: In which situation is a model's knowledge cutoff most likely to produce harmful output without any visible error signal?

options.A: When the model is asked to generate creative or fictional content drawing on historical themes
options.B: When the prompt explicitly instructs the model to flag any information it is uncertain about
options.C: When the model is asked about a domain that has changed significantly since its cutoff, and the output is fluent and assertive about the now-outdated state
options.D: When the model is given a source document in context that itself predates the knowledge cutoff

items.question: What risk arises when reviewers verify only the claims they personally recognise as checkable, rather than following a systematic protocol?

options.A: The review will take significantly longer than planned, reducing the number of items covered in the allotted time
options.B: The model detects the reviewer's domain expertise and adjusts its output to make unfamiliar domain claims harder to verify
options.C: Reviewers will focus on the lowest-risk claims because those are the easiest to confirm quickly
options.D: High-risk claims in domains outside the reviewer's expertise are systematically excluded from verification, creating a blind spot proportional to the reviewer's knowledge gaps

items.question: What is the primary mechanism by which retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) reduces hallucination risk?

options.A: RAG provides current, specific source documents in context, giving the model factual material to generate from rather than relying solely on parametric memory
options.B: RAG replaces the model's language generation with direct document retrieval, so no generation occurs for factual claims
options.C: RAG applies a post-generation filter that removes hallucinated claims by comparing them to retrieved documents
options.D: RAG continuously updates the model's parametric memory with newly retrieved documents, eliminating staleness

items.question: Why can a model's self-review of its own output not substitute for independent human verification?

options.A: Models are architecturally unable to process their own output as an input in the same session
options.B: The model may reproduce the same systematic errors in its self-review that appeared in its original output, providing no independent check
options.C: Model self-review is computationally expensive and substantially increases latency for the user
options.D: Regulatory frameworks generally prohibit using AI to assess AI-generated content in professional contexts

items.question: Which TWO characteristics make an error in a model-generated legal or regulatory reference especially dangerous? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Legal references are always longer than other output types, increasing the cost of review
options.B: Legal documents are written in technical language that correlates with higher model accuracy
options.C: Acting on an incorrect regulatory reference can produce irreversible compliance consequences before the error is detected
options.D: Legal references are more likely to be fabricated than other claim types because legal text appears frequently in training data
options.E: Errors in regulatory references are often expressed in plausible technical language that reviewers without legal expertise may not recognise as wrong

items.question: What distinguishes an omission error that is a functional failure from one that merely reduces completeness?

options.A: A functional omission involves missing structured fields; a completeness omission involves missing supplementary narrative
options.B: A functional omission occurs in summaries; a completeness omission occurs in structured extractions
options.C: A functional omission is detectable through source-to-output comparison; a completeness omission is not detectable
options.D: A functional omission leaves out information a consumer needs to act correctly or safely; a completeness omission leaves out detail that would enrich the output but does not change how it is acted upon

items.question: Which TWO statements correctly describe how verification accountability should be assigned in a shared model workflow? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Each team member who acts on model output is primarily accountable for verifying that output before using it in their own work
options.B: The team member who originally configured the workflow is accountable for verifying all outputs the workflow produces, regardless of who uses them
options.C: Accountability can be formally assigned to a designated reviewer role, provided that role performs substantive checks before output is acted upon by any team member
options.D: When multiple parties use the same output, accountability transfers to the last person who handled it before the decision was made
options.E: Accountability is shared equally across all team members with access to the workflow, regardless of who acted on specific outputs

items.question: In what circumstance is the absence of hedging language in model output most likely to mislead a reviewer?

options.A: When the model was prompted to write in a formal, authoritative style that structurally suppresses uncertainty markers
options.B: When the model expresses high confidence about a specific claim it fabricated, because the fabrication and the assertive tone are products of the same generation process
options.C: When the reviewer has domain expertise and expects confident assertion from a high-quality source
options.D: When the model's training data for the topic is rich and enables highly developed assertive patterns

items.question: What is the primary risk when verification samples are selected by the reviewer because items 'looked typical' rather than drawn randomly?

options.A: Atypical items — which may include edge cases with higher error rates — are systematically excluded from review coverage
options.B: Typical items take longer to review because they require comparison against a broader range of source documents
options.C: The model produces more errors in atypical items but these are usually discarded without being acted upon
options.D: Regulatory requirements mandate random sampling and prohibit judgment-based selection in AI output verification

items.question: Why is verifying a model's claim by asking the model a follow-up question about the same topic an unreliable verification method?

options.A: Follow-up questions cause the model to reset its context, losing access to the original claim
options.B: Models always produce different answers on follow-up questions, making comparison impossible
options.C: Follow-up questions are interpreted as instructions to revise the original output rather than to verify it
options.D: The model may produce consistent but wrong answers across multiple turns because the same error patterns persist across its responses to related queries

items.question: Which TWO properties of numerical claims make them especially prone to propagating undetected errors? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Precise figures (percentages, dollar amounts, counts) read as authoritative and are often accepted and forwarded without independent calculation verification
options.B: Numerical claims always come paired with a named source citation, making them easier to verify than qualitative claims
options.C: Models systematically produce incorrect numerical claims more frequently than incorrect qualitative claims
options.D: Numerical claims can be incorporated into downstream calculations or decisions, causing a small error to compound into a substantially larger consequential error
options.E: Numerical claims always involve parametric memory because models cannot perform arithmetic on context-window data

items.question: What does it mean for a claim in model output to be 'verifiable' in the context of output evaluation?

options.A: The claim was produced from source material that was present in the model's context window
options.B: The claim can be checked against an independent source of ground truth that exists outside the model's output
options.C: The claim uses sufficiently precise language to be unambiguous in its interpretation
options.D: The claim was reviewed and confirmed correct by a human reviewer before use

items.question: What is the primary purpose of checking model output for internal consistency?

options.A: To verify that the model used the same citation format throughout the document
options.B: To confirm that the model followed all formatting constraints specified in the prompt
options.C: To detect cases where the model contradicts itself within the same output, which signals reasoning or coherence errors
options.D: To ensure the output length falls within the target word count specified in the prompt

items.question: A verification workflow designed for one task type is applied without modification to a meaningfully different task. What specific risk does this create?

options.A: The review will take longer because reviewers are unfamiliar with the new task's output format
options.B: The model will produce lower quality output for the new task type, increasing error rates but not changing which errors the workflow checks for
options.C: The documentation requirements for the new task may differ from those the workflow was designed for
options.D: The workflow may have blind spots for error types characteristic of the new task that were not present in the original task the workflow was designed around

items.question: What is the primary concern when a verification team draws samples from a batch based on which items appear to look similar to prior correct outputs?

options.A: The sample will systematically under-represent items that are different from prior outputs — which is where new error types are most likely to appear
options.B: Similar-looking items take longer to review because the reviewer must explain why they are similar
options.C: The model produces more errors in items similar to prior output because those patterns are over-represented in training data
options.D: Selecting based on similarity to prior correct outputs violates data minimisation principles under applicable privacy frameworks

items.question: Why does grounding a model's claim in a secondary source rather than a primary source increase residual verification risk?

options.A: Secondary sources are generally excluded from Project knowledge under standard data governance policies
options.B: Grounding in a secondary source is structurally equivalent to producing an ungrounded claim, because the primary source is not in context
options.C: A secondary source may have misrepresented, selectively reported, or misquoted the primary source, adding an error layer between the claim and the underlying fact
options.D: Secondary sources are typically older than the primary sources they reference, introducing compounded staleness risk

items.question: Which TWO are valid techniques for specifically reducing omission errors in model-generated summaries? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Providing the model with a strict word limit to force prioritisation of the most important content
options.B: Asking the model to rate its own confidence in the completeness of the summary after generating it
options.C: Instructing the model to list all key findings or topics before writing the narrative summary, enabling a completeness check against the listing
options.D: Using a higher model tier for the summarisation task
options.E: After receiving the summary, comparing it item-by-item against the source document to identify content in the source that is absent from the summary

items.question: What is the key limitation of using a fixed checklist to verify model output against quality criteria?

options.A: A checklist can only catch errors of types the checklist designers anticipated; novel or unexpected error types fall entirely outside its scope
options.B: Checklists require the reviewer to assess every item sequentially, which prevents efficient batching of similar checks
options.C: Checklists cannot be used for tasks involving numerical claims because numbers require calculation, not checklist comparison
options.D: Checklists require extensive documentation of each checklist item's result, adding review time without improving coverage

items.question: Why does providing source documents in context reduce hallucination risk without eliminating the need for independent verification?

options.A: The model can still misread, selectively quote, or misrepresent the source documents it was given, even when those documents are present in context
options.B: Source documents provided in context are not accessible to human reviewers, so verification cannot use the same sources the model saw
options.C: Providing source documents increases context window length, which proportionally increases the probability of generation errors
options.D: Independent verification is only required when source documents are not provided in context

items.question: In a verification workflow, what distinguishes the check that detects staleness from the check that detects fabrication?

options.A: Staleness is detected by comparing the output against itself for internal consistency; fabrication is detected by comparing output against external sources
options.B: Staleness is detected by comparing output against current sources that postdate the model's training; fabrication is detected by confirming the cited source exists and says what the model claims
options.C: Staleness is detected by automated tools that cross-reference against training data snapshots; fabrication requires human judgment to confirm
options.D: Both are detected by the same check: comparing output against any available system of record

items.question: How does good model calibration affect the practical design of a sampling-based verification strategy?

options.A: Good calibration eliminates the need for random sampling because confidently-stated claims can be assumed correct
options.B: Good calibration allows reviewers to skip all hedged items because uncertainty markers reliably indicate incorrect claims
options.C: Good calibration allows hedging signals to serve as a useful prioritisation guide within a fixed sample, without eliminating coverage of confident claims
options.D: Good calibration makes any sampling rate produce equally reliable quality estimates regardless of the task's stake level

items.question: In what specific way can a knowledge-cutoff staleness error produce a functional omission error in the same output?

options.A: Staleness errors always produce omission errors simultaneously because outdated content is always shorter than current content
options.B: A staleness error produces an omission when the model's parametric memory has been fully replaced by newer information, leaving a gap in the output
options.C: Staleness and omission errors are mutually exclusive because a stale assertion occupies the same space a correct statement would, leaving no gap
options.D: A staleness error can produce a functional omission when the outdated assertion suppresses mention of a current development the consumer needs in order to act correctly

items.question: When a fabricated claim from model output is copied into multiple downstream documents by different users, what is the accountability principle for verification of each instance?

options.A: Each individual who incorporates the claim into their own work is responsible for verifying it before doing so
options.B: Accountability rests solely with the person who prompted the original output that contained the fabrication
options.C: No individual bears accountability once a claim has been incorporated into organisational documents and treated as established fact
options.D: The organisation bears collective accountability, eliminating individual responsibility for verification

items.question: How does verification documentation support investigation when a model output error is discovered after the output has been used?

options.A: Documentation allows the model to retrace its generation steps and identify where the error originated in the parametric memory
options.B: Documentation establishes what was checked, by whom, and when — enabling investigators to determine whether verification was adequate and where accountability lies
options.C: Documentation automatically triggers re-verification of the output by comparing it against the stored review record
options.D: Documentation prevents further propagation of the error by flagging all downstream documents that incorporated the verified output

items.question: A model synthesises three source documents and accurately reproduces a factual error present in one of them. Which combination of properties describes this specific claim?

options.A: Ungrounded and inaccurate, because the model reproduced an error rather than the ground truth
options.B: Grounded and accurate, because the model faithfully represented the source material it was given
options.C: Grounded and inaccurate, because the claim traces to a context source but that source itself contains a factual error
options.D: Ungrounded and accurate, because a claim that is wrong cannot be considered properly grounded
